name: Manga Buang
confidence_why: Every description of Manga Buang stress comes from one SIL fieldwork team, Hardwick and Healey 1965, Healey 1967 and the 2007 SIL phonology data checked by Healey, and all three place stress on the antepenultimate and final syllables with long non-central vowels attracting it, differing only on whether stress ever contrasts, though Healey 1967 herself calls stress very difficult to hear.

However it seems that words tend to have ante-penultimate stress with a secondary ultimate stress, and two syllable words have ultimate stress. Stress may be pulled forward to a preceeding syllable with a long vowel if the syllable which is usually stressed has a short vowel.[4] Thus there are the following word patterns: 'mora'bir 'type of bird'[5] / pa'se:pis 'fern' / ba'gak 'moth' / 'de:dis 'wasp'. new_statements.quote: Stress is often very difficult to distinguish, especially on words spoken in isolation. However it seems that words tend to have ante-penultimate stress with a secondary ultimate stress, and two syllable words have ultimate stress. Stress may be pulled forward to a preceeding syllable with a long vowel if the syllable which is usually stressed has a short vowel.[fn 4: Lengthened a seems to have less power to do this than do other lengthened vowels.] Thus there are the following word patterns: 'mora'bir 'type of bird', pa'se:pis 'fern', ba'gak 'moth', 'de:dis 'wasp'. Four syllable words do not follow this pattern as regularly ... Stress appears to contrast in a few words: ni'paya 'bad', 'nibasa 'good'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and phonetically weak. Default: primary stress on the antepenult with a secondary stress on the final syllable (words of 3+ syllables); disyllables are stressed on the final syllable. Vowel length overrides position: a long (especially non-/a/) vowel attracts the stress away from a short normally-stressed syllable (OPD 2007 by the same author: 'a syllable with a long non-central vowel is always stressed'). The 1965 phonemic statement phrases the same system as 'a tendency to last and third to last stress in all words' with length/quality-conditioned sub-rules.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the final (ultimate) syllable of words with antepenultimate primary stress; some four-syllable words keep two stressed syllables even inside utterances (p. 4); roughly equal timing between word nuclei.
new_statements.exceptions: Four-syllable words irregular (role of affixation/compounding unsolved); a few apparent minimal stress contrasts (ni'paya 'bad' vs 'nibasa 'good'); 1965 statement lists lexical exceptions ('nabu'nabu 'itchy', 'mari'kani place name, 'pasi'daka 'very small', reduplicated 'baga'baga) and two words stressed on /j/-initial syllables; monosyllabic suffixes always stressed (1965, rule b); lengthened /a:/ attracts stress less than other long vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (one stressed nucleus plus up to four marginal syllables), which need not coincide with the grammatical word; patterns are stated for citation forms and the authors warn that 'the stress patterns on many of these words change as they are included in phrases' (fn. 6 gives examples); phrase nucleus usually on the phrase-final syllable (Part I p. 11). All statements hedged as tentative ('tend to', 'nowhere very forceful').
new_statements.identity_note: All three primary sources describe the speech of Mangga (Manga) village at the SW (Mumeng) end of the Snake River valley, i.e. Mangga Buang proper (mang1404), which the authors explicitly distinguish from the other two 'dialects' (Central/Mapos and headwaters Buang = mapo1242). The archive.org 'Buang Dictionary' (Hooley 2006) also saved in the folder is Mapos/Central Buang (mapo1242), not the target; it is kept only as a related-language note.

new_statements.quote: No contrastive stress pairs have been found and stress is nowhere very forceful. There is a tendency to last and third to last stress in all words, with the following exceptions. In the following paragraphs, /V/ refers to any vowel except /a/, and /V:/ refers to any lengthened vowel except /a:/. (a) Two syllable words have first stress when (i) the first syllable contains /V/, /V:/ or /a:/ and the second syllable is open, (ii) there is /V:/ in the first syllable but not in the final closed syllable. [...] (c) In three syllable words the second syllable is stressed when it contains /a:/ compared with /a/ in another syllable, or /V:/ compared with /V/ or /a/ in another syllable. The final or first syllable also remains stressed if it contains /V:/ or /a:/.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's existing 1967 part II statement (antepenultimate + ultimate; long vowels attract stress) but earlier, explicit that stress is non-contrastive and weak, and spells out the vowel-weight conditions by word length, plus listed exceptions. Minor tension: 1965 finds no contrastive stress pairs; 1967 part II says stress 'appears to contrast in a few words' (ni'paya 'bad' vs 'nibasa 'good'). Rules (a)-(e) quoted from scanned of pp. 41-42 (a render queue on the box prevented re-checking those two page images); the p. 40 deciding sentences were verified on the page image.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and weak. Default: final and antepenultimate syllables stressed in all words. Weight overrides: in disyllables the first syllable is stressed if it has a non-central or long vowel and the second is open, or if it has a long vowel and the closed final does not; stressed monosyllabic suffixes shift disyllable stress to the first syllable unless the second has a long vowel; in trisyllables a long-vowel (or /a:/ vs /a/) second syllable takes stress and a long-vowel first or final syllable keeps stress; in four-syllable words a first syllable with /V/, /V:/ or /a:/ is stressed rather than a second syllable with /V/ or /a/.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not named as such; the default is two stressed syllables per word (last and third-from-last), and rule (c) allows a long-vowel first or final syllable to 'remain stressed' beside a stressed second syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Rule (e): 'Exceptions to these rules include two words which are stressed on syllables commencing with /j/, and the following words for which there is no obvious explanation' (e.g. /navunabu/ 'itchy', /ma:rikani/ place name, /pasidaka/ 'very small', /vagabaga/ 'different kinds'). Footnote 8 (p. 52): 'It is hoped that further investigation will lead to a simpler explanation for the occurrences of stress.'
new_statements.identity_note: All six works describe Mangga (Manga) Buang, the Mumeng / south-western dialect of Buang in the Snake River valley, Morobe District, which Hardwick and Healey treat as a separate language (ISO mmo, ~2,000 speakers; data from the village of Mangga, 1963-66). The Hooley 2006 Buang dictionary already held by the project is Mapos/Central Buang (mapo1242), not this language, and was not used.

readall_conflicts: No source disagrees on placement: every statement (1965 tentative phonemic statement; 1967 phonological hierarchy part II already in the catalog; the 2007 SIL Organised Phonology Data held by the project) puts stress on the antepenultimate and the final syllable, with final stress in disyllables and long (non-central) vowels attracting stress. Two small tensions between the 1965 and 1967 papers by the same authors: (i) 1965 reports 'no contrastive stress pairs have been found' and calls stress non-contrastive, while 1967 part II says stress 'appears to contrast in a few words' (ni'paya 'bad' vs 'nibasa 'good') though it still treats stress as largely predictable and hard to hear; (ii) 1965 states the default as 'last and third to last stress in all words' without ranking them and gives disyllables initial stress under vowel-weight conditions, whereas 1967 ranks antepenultimate as primary with secondary ultimate and says disyllables have ultimate stress (with long vowels pulling stress forward). The 1965 weight rules are the more detailed and are compatible with 1967's long-vowel override. The remaining four works (Healey 1977, 1967 clauses, 1984 topic continuity; Hardwick 1967 part I, 1970 sentences) are silent on word stress and only describe phrase- or sentence-final intonation.

sources.note: Sec. 1 'Phonological Word', pp. 2-4: word = one stressed nuclear syllable plus marginals; stress weak (slight intensity/length/high pitch), hard to hear in isolation; words tend to have antepenultimate stress with secondary ultimate stress, disyllables ultimate; stress pulled to a preceding long-vowel syllable if the normally stressed syllable is short (fn.4: lengthened a has less power to do this); four-syllable words irregular; apparent contrast ni'paya 'bad' vs 'nibasa 'good'; stress patterns change in phrases (fn.6 examples).
